I'm sure this will be one of many responses, but I feel like jumping
in on this one. The clearest distinctions are the in-clan disciplines
for the two respective clans. The Femur duplicates effects from
several Vicissitude cards and is a decent but not overly large combat
boost to the few Tzimisce that are low on Vicissitude. Contrast to
the Assamites, who have Celerity in-clan. Quietus is their
discipline-based source of agg damage, but the Fang is a MASSIVE boost
to Assamites who are low on Quietus but do have Celerity, since
Celerity works VERY well with weapons (auspex and animalism less so).
Also, the Assamites, unlike the Tzimisce, have Obfuscate in-clan. The
ability to Disguise an agg-dealing hand weapon is a pretty big bonus
in and of itself.

To summarize:
Tzimisce + Femur = "Meh, I expect them to do that anyway"
Assamites + Fang = "RUN AWAY!"

See also:
Discussions on cost of Opium Den.

Eric Simon
Prince of Chicago

That is a reasonable question that I have never actually seen
addressed before. My initial thought was that there was a subtle
difference (maybe one was a melee weapon and the other isn't), but in
fact, they are identical in all ways except cost and clan. There are a
few possible reasons:

1. Kali's Fang was printed before Femur. It is possible that Kali's
Fang was costed at 3, and then the designers of the Sabbat expansion
(who were probably different folks than the designers of the AH
expansion where Kali's Fang was published) figured that 3 pool was
simply too expensive for that sort of weapon, and made the Femur 2,
figuring that the disparity wasn't a big deal, and then no one ever
cared to fix the Fang.

2. Someone figured that the assamites needed to pay more pool for
their weapon than the Tzimiscee (much like the Gangrel have to pay 2
pool for Backways where the Nosferatu only have to pay 1 for an
identical ability).

In the end, I'm assuming that Fang was costed at 3 pool as opposed to
2 pool, as Fang is just better than Sengir Dagger (which did strength
aggro damage where Fang does strength +1 aggro) but then whomever
designed Femur figured that the conditional cost of needing X clan was
sufficient to make up for the difference and made it cost 2 pool
instead of 3, and Fang was just overlooked or simply left behind.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Jesper wrote:
> Mainly, I belive, coz they arent the same weapon.

For all intents and purposes, they are.

> There are a BIG difference
> there, one being a Tchmizc the other being a Assamite weapon.

Which might be a reasonable argument if they both didn't have access
to reliable aggro damage.

When you look at The Labyrinth vs Back Ways, it makes sense that The
Labyrinth costs only 1 pool, 'cause the Nosferatu have more stealth
than you can shake a stick at, where the Gangrel have limited stealth.
Thus, the Gangrel pay more for the Back Ways. Makes sense. Femur and
Fang, however, are both weapons given to clans that have the same
access to aggro damage, more or less.

>You can ask
> you same the question, why so "Earth Control" cost one blood when "Lost in
> Crows" cost nothing, that they dose the same.

That is easy and sensible--Obfuscate hands out stealth like crazy.
There are more Obfuscate cards that hand out stealth than any other
type of Obfuscate card. Protean, on the other hand, is not so stealth
rich--there are, what, 3 cards that give stealth to Protean? One is
unrestricted, one is multi purpose, and one only grants stealth at
superior. And all three cost blood.

If Kali's Fang was, say, a Malkavian weapon (Malkavians having no
combat disciplines and limited access to combat abilities), then the 3
pool would make sense. But for the Assamites, who are primarily a
combat clan and have easy access to aggrivated damage already, making
Fang cost 3 pool when Femur costs 2 smacks of glitch.

> I belive if you can ask that
> question, and understand why there is a difference you will understand why
> there is a difference in Kalis vs. Toomler, if its fair its another
> question.

The Lost in Crowds vs Earth Control (or Majesty vs Earth Meld or Read
Intentions vs Dodge) makes perfect sense, given the context of the
abilies and powers granted. On the other hand, Kali's Fang vs Femur
strike me as a pretty clear case of the mysterious game design that
plagued the early expansions--Femur of Toomler is probably costed
correctly for both weapons, but no one figured it was worth the effort
to fix Kali's Fang.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

"Ulugh Beg II" <dontfe...@spam.me> wrote

> It's kinda weird if you compare it so a Sengir Dagger though.

Not so much--Sengir Dagger does strength aggro. Femur/Fang do strength
+1 aggro, which is significant.

That Femur/Fang have a significant conditional cost (i.e. clan
specific) should be enough to justify the improvement. In the case of
Femur, it is sufficient (Femur costs 2 pool, just like Sengir, but
does +1 damage). In the case of Fang, the conditionality is not
sufficient.

I suspect this is an oversight/error/glitch more than a specific
design idea.

> It's the same old issue of comparing the Ivory Bow to ANY other weapon.
> Then again, the bow gets contested every single game...

I dunno. Ivory Bow seems reasonable when compared to 38 Special--38
costs 1 pool, gives you a manuver, does 1 damage, is not unique. Ivory
Bow costs 1 pool, does 1 aggro damage. No manuver. Is unique. Seems
pretty close, balance wise.

-Peter

My take on the costing is:

If it's something the clan can do anyway, with multiple cards, then
it's the location / equipment is really just a diffent option to do
what they do anyway (labyrinth, opium den)

Femur gives close range agg, which the Tzim already had. It also
requires an equip action, cos Tzim aren't flush with obf.

If it's something that costs pool or is restricted, then the location
/ equipment is extending their capabilities a bit more meaningfully,
and should cost more. Most Gangrel stealth costs them, so Backaways
fits that description. Most Lasombra stealth costs, or has
resrtictions, so Elysian Fields fits that description.

Fang gives close range agg, which the Assimites don't otherwise have.
They can whip it out with disguised weapon, which is not an option for
the Tzim. It (and weapons in general) also give them a non-card
intensive combat option, which they didn't otherwise have... compare
wasting zero cards to strike with the Fang and have it Majestied,
compared to wasting a Flash, a Taste of Death (and a blood).

halc...@aol.com (Halcyan 2) wrote:

> A lot harder to burn with Sengir Dagger since it only does strength damage. You

Sure, but that doesn't explain why Fang is 3 pool where Femur is 2
pool. Fang lets you burn folks. So does Femur. The Assamites can Blur
(or whatever) to do the neccessary extra damage. The Tzimiscee can use
Horrid Form or Blood of Acid or Carrion Crows to do the extra damage.
It strikes me as kind of a wash.

> Yeah, but it's only the Horrid Form decks that can effectively use the Femur >in
> such a fashion. Any Assamite deck using CEL can use the Fang to deadly effect.

And any Tsimiscee deck can use Horrid Form or Carrion Crows of Blood
of Acid to do effectively the same thing.

> Yes they are.

No, no, you misunderstand me. The Gangrel pay more for Backways 'cause
it provides them with a rarer effect--it is harder for the Gangrel to
get stealth through their disciplines than it is for the Nosferatu to
get stealth in the same way. Thus, the increased cost. That makes
sense. The Gangrel are not, however, more *powerful* (in the sense of
more destructive, or whatever) with that +1 stealth than the Nosferatu
are. That +1 stealth from the Backways is not allowing the Gangrel to
be more destructive than the Nosferatu--the post I was responding to
suggested that the Fang cost 3 instead of 2 'cause the Assamites could
cause more damage than the Tzimiscee (i.e. they were more powerful
with the Fang), so the added destruction justified the added cost. As
all other instances of greater cost for similar ability read, the
increased cost comes from the scarcity of the ability relative to the
context--i.e. Earth Control costs 1 blood where Lost in Crowds does
not, as EC is a stealth card in a primarily combat discipline (much
like Alacrity costs 2 blood for a similar effect--stealth is even
further removed from Celerity). On the other hand, clans that have
access to such abilities freely get things cheaper--look at the
various Brujah/!Brujah weapons--they are relatively cheap for what
they do, even though the Brujah can use them to great effect. The
Brujah get these things *cheaper* than other clans, not more
expensively.

> As others have noted, Protean stealth is costlier than Obfuscate
> stealth (Earth Control vs. Lost in Crowds).

Yeah--others like me :-)

-Peter

have access to Claws of the Dead and the Nosferatu not so much does
not make the +1 stealth granted by Backways more powerful than the
Nosferatu's +1 stealth as granted by the Labyrinth.

Backways costs 2 instead of 1, presumably, 'cause the Gangrel have
only limited access to stealth--a few cards that cost blood in
Protean, generally speaking. Thus it makes sense that Backways costs
more than Labyrinth, as the Nosferatu are oozing stealth.

Fang, on the other hand, gives the Assamites an ability that is very
similar to the ability to that which Femur gives the Tzimiscee--they

be made that Fang costs more 'cause the Assamites have limited access
to *close range* aggro damage that Fang provides, but strikes me as a

I'd still think that Fang costs 3 and Femur costs 2 due to, primarily,
oversight.

-Peter

Messages.Author: David Cherryholmes
Messages.Body:
On 29 Oct 2003, Peter D Bakija wrote:

> All the working Assamite combat decks I have seen involved long range
> and Taste of Death (after Blood Sweat beatings).

But how *well* have they worked, that's the question. I'll grant you that
most the Assamite decks you've seen probably did home in on Blood
Sweat/Taste of Death, but I wouldn't equate "cards got played" with
"working". Working means winning, in my book.

I know you know that I'm an Assamite fan. I've been working on this
theory for a while, and started a thread on www.thepathofblood.com called
"Quietus: a dangerous distraction?". Initially the reaction was poor but
when some of the good players went back and took stock of what Assamite
decks they played that could win tables, they found a common thread: very
little if any Quietus at all.

Strike cards eat up card slots. Conditional strike cards eat up even more
card slots. It would be better to not eat up card slots at all, and
instead devote them to ousting and not being ousted (in a more direct
sense than the combat itself you are running does). Virtually all the
Assamites have CEL. As you know, CEL coupled with any constant damage
source greater than a single point is *good*, and even the hands-for-one
isn't bad (3 points of damage being a benchmark of sorts for a good
combat). So, who are the star Assamites?

Parnassus: +1 str, and can Magic of the Smith the perfect weapon for that
table.

Fatima: built in Disguised Weapon

Thetmes: agg hands, might as well have a Sengir, only better

Parmenides: +1 Str

Tegyrius: +1 Str

Kalinda, Zahir, Sluggy, Al-Ashrad: Magic of the Smith

Bajezet: Claws of the Dead special

Tariq: you end up wanting him to have a weapon for different reasons,
same result.

Who else would you want to play? The noteable exception is Jalal, with
his *other* card-saving special, Psyche. He is the one I would single out
as making the long-range stuff worth it, but he is a lone vampire.

> Yeah, you have to get
> to long range, but the Assamites have no problem at all doing that
> with Flash and Pursuit, both of which can be used in significant
> amounts with no adverse effect on deck function.

But they do have an adverse effect. They eat up *a lot* of card slots,
leaving you with not much else.

> Yeah, that kind of
> deck gets tooled by DOtB, but DoTB tools Kali's Fang too.

This is a myth. Handing someone with CEL +1 Str is not "tooling" them,
unless you mean "tooling up". It might still be a better deal for the
DotB player, but it doesn't adversly affect the Assamite deck that
much.

>And
> occasionally you get stuck against a deck that can set range, but
> those are very few and far between.

Agreed. We should ignore cornercases for the purposes of this discussion.

> Thus, it strikes me as perfectly
> reasonable to refer to Taste of Death as "oozing" :-)

You are simply describing what you've seen, which I can't and won't
dispute. I, OTOH, am trying to advocate a better way to play Assamites.

> I've never seen a single Blood Agony get played. Ever. But Taste of
> Death? Every single time I see the Assamites. Which is fairly often,
> really.

Well, they are rare Ancient Hearts cards, right? If I had more, I'd play
them. I have played the four I own, in the past. Once again, that +1
Str/CEL makes that card really good, and you can use it with a weapon,
too. Seriously, I think it's the rarity that's at issue here.

> Really? What are you playing against? IG Rush decks get trumped,
> generally speaking, by Assamite combat, as the Assamites have more
> manuvers, generally speaking (or they should, as they wan't long
> range). Other combat decks aren't going to have so much manuver. Non
> combat decks aren't going to have the manuvers either.

Yeah, really (and I'm a pig-headed SOB). It was more of a metagame thing,
personally. Players adapted to my long range strike-ishness and I had to
move on. After I moved on for those reasons, I sort of stumbled on
non-quietus decks by accident and started noticing a trend, which got me
thinking....

> Well, yes, S:CE and Obedience are a problem, but not one that is
> solved by Kali's Fang, such that the extra pool cost is justified.

But with a weapon you haven't wasted a card slot and possibly blood. That
was another thing that got me on the path of building the types of
Assamite decks I have been lately: our answers to S:CE are mediocre, at
best. Therefore, never waste a strike card by never playing a strike
card, and it won't be so bad.

> I've seen regular Assamite Rush at long range (Flash/Pursuit, Blood
> Sweat, Taste of Death, Psyche! when necessary) work pretty well--It
> isn't fantastic (much like any mid range vampire Rush deck), but is
> pretty trumpy, combat wise, and does ok.

I'm shooting for a little better than "ok" and the Quietus strikes weren't
doing it for me, personally. Lord knows I tried.



Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Wouter Kuyper wrote:
> I think indeed that the Backways is more powerfull than the Labyrinth,
> exactly following your reasoning....if you give Gangrells the same
> easy access to stealth as the Nosferatu + easy acces to other things
> (like aggro-handdamage) while you leave the nosferatu with nothing but
> their stealth, then i am sure the Gangrell come out of that comparison
> as the stronger one...

While this isn't really relevant to the actual discussion at hand,
I'll ask anyway--really, what are the Gangrel going to do with that +1
stealth that is so scary? They can't bleed that much. They have access
to transient stealth already, along with the incredibly potent Form of
Mist. They already scare folks away from blocking by virtue of having
Protean. The extra +1 stealth from the Backways? Not that big a deal.
Handy, sure. Reasonably priced at 2 pool? Absolutely. But I'm *so* not
seeing the Gangrel as being more *powerful* with the +1 stealth.

Stealth is harder to come by for the Gangrel than the Nosferatu, and
while it makes sense that getting it is more expensive, it hardly
makes them scary.

> So you must make sure that the Gangrell have more difficulties with
> getting stealth, hence the difference in cost for the locations.

Not so much seeing it.

> I think the same can be said for the two weapons. The Assamites don't
> have easy access to closerange-aggro, while the Tzim do,..giving the
> Asses that option should be more expensive.

Why do the Assamites even *want* close range aggro? At close range,
the Assamites get hit back. At close range, the Assamites get
Immortally Grappled (which the Fang certainly doesn't help them
against). The Assamites can easily get long range, and once there,
they can wail on folks with Blood Sweat and Taste of Death (both of
which are easy to get and plentiful). Close range is not somehwere
they want to be. Yeah, S:CE is a problem for the Assamites, but being
at close range isn't going to help them there, and S:CE is going to be
just as much of a problem for a Fang weilding Assamite as it is a long
range Taste of Death Assamite.

> I think it is logical, but maybe in this case not necessary, or
> overcompensated...3 pool is just too much for what it does

Agreed that 3 pool is just too much.

-Peter

Me too. At 2, I suspect that you are putting Sengir Dagger in every

still hosed by S:CE, and that 1 pool savings isn't going to, like,
make them sweep tables any more.

> Er, I mean.... "Scott! Take notice of the majority of two! Stop keeping
> the Assamite bruthah down!"

Fight the Power!

-Peter

Somebody on pathofblood said I was just going through a phase. Maybe I

> Lucky Blow to make Femur burn someone. And yet they are still only

Good point.

> Assamite deck you build.

I only have three right now. One uses Thetmes, another is The Fatimator
and is all about AR's, but the last is "dial a weapon". It originally had
the dagger in lieu of the fang, but I actually traded up. The deck
defends it's pool pretty well so the extra cost seemed negligible, and
there's some goodness in having multiple strikes and a way to do either 2
or 3 points of damage. With agg in the mix it's a much more controllable
burn.

> The +1 damage is a defenite bonus, but

See that 2/3 thing above.

> In practice, I think you are correct, but I think in terms of design,
> 1 is probably about right (it probably should be about 1.5, but it has
> to be rounded somwhere).

I think it's easily worth two. Theoretically, it usually takes building a
deck around that goal to actually burn anyone, whether you are doing one
or two points of agg (diablerie being the most common case, and again
making the 1 or 2 question moot). Practically, everyone plays with
it; that doesn't necessarily make it *too* good, but it's clearly a good
deal if so many players choose to use it.

> True, but in the original set, there was a significant cost increase
> given to things that could burn vampires (look at Flame
> Thrower)--Ivory Bow can *never* burn anyone (well, except in some,
> like, Dawn Op/Carrion Crows/Ivory Bow combo), where Dagger as a melee
> weapon certainly can.

Hey, this just occurred to me. It's really just another way of making the
"design team on crack" argument, but... was the Fang designed during the
window where one agg could burn you? If it was, and the Femur was
released after things went back to the original/current rules, that would
explain some of the costing.

> Eh. You really think it is going to make the Assamites *that* much
> better? I mean, as it is, they can freely burn vampires, but for S:CE.

I'd still dispute that "freely" bit. But even if that strategy were
perfectly reliable, it's just a *huge* chain of cards; if you can get that
kind of card flow then "freely" burning vampires is appropriate. CEL is a
force muliplyer, so every extra point you add to the base damage makes a
big difference in the damage-per-round. That and the fact that I rarely
carry just one weapon; if I'm dialing up three strikes, I'd much rather
have some options.

> Fang, costing 2, will save them some card slots, sure, but they are
> still hosed by S:CE,

You've got it backwards. *Because* they are saving card slots, it is more
probable that they *won't* get hosed by S:CE. The problem now becomes
grapple, but Sideslip and Guardian Angel and Flak Jacket (if you've got
the time) are your friends.

> and that 1 pool savings isn't going to, like,
> make them sweep tables any more.

Depending on your playstyle, it may. Remember that I lowball the poolgain
a fair bit and let myself drop perilously close to being ousted. But
sure, I don't think 1 point either way is a big deal, generally.



Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

David Cherryholmes wrote:
> I think it's easily worth two. Theoretically, it usually takes building a
> deck around that goal to actually burn anyone, whether you are doing one
> or two points of agg (diablerie being the most common case, and again
> making the 1 or 2 question moot). Practically, everyone plays with
> it; that doesn't necessarily make it *too* good, but it's clearly a good
> deal if so many players choose to use it.

I think the Ivory Bow could have been costed at 2, and it still would
have been as pobular as it is, but I think in the grand scheme of
things, it costing 1 is not out of the realm of logic. 38 Special
costs 1 and does 1 non aggrivated damage and gives you a manuver.
Ivory Bow costs 1, does 1 aggrivated damage, does not give you a
manuver, and is unique. The question is whether no manuver and unique
is a balanced trade with aggrivated damage. Heck, if the aggro damage
is worth 2 points, the hypothetical math works out:

38 Special: 1 pool (-1), 1R damage (+1), manuver (+1)= 1
Ivory Bow: 1 pool (-1), 1R damage (+1), unique (-1), aggro damage
(+2)= 1

Heck, the math is sketchy, but possibly illustrates how Ivory Bow
costs 1 pool. On the other hand, I agree with you that Ivory Bow
probably should have been 2 pool :-)

On the other hand, using the same logic, I'm not quite seeing how
Sengir Dagger costs 2 pool...

> Hey, this just occurred to me. It's really just another way of making the
> "design team on crack" argument, but... was the Fang designed during the
> window where one agg could burn you? If it was, and the Femur was
> released after things went back to the original/current rules, that would
> explain some of the costing.

They both came out after the VTES rulebook changed the aggro rules to
"1 point of aggro will burn you", but before they were changed back.

I suspect that the real culprit here is that Fang originally did 2
aggro damage, instead of "strength +1" (although the Femur's original
text was "+1 aggrivated hand damage..."), and somehow that justified
it's 3 pool cost.

More than anything, however, it think it is, in fact, the direct
result of the crack.

-Peter

of someone else equipping theirs first and deny you the opportunity to use
yours, the opposite is also true (if you get yours first, noone else will be

advantage in most cases.

Messages.Author: The Fanboy
Messages.Body:
>Makes sense. Femur and Fang, however, are both weapons given to clans
that >have the same access to aggro damage, more or less.

Here's a comparison of Assamite to Tzimice close-range aggravated
damage sources, using only cards available when the two weapons were
printed.

Assamites: Blood Agony. Second round only.

Taste of Death doesn't count because it can't be used at close. So
the Assamites have all of one source of close range aggravated damage,
and it can't be played on the first round.

Tzimice: Blood of Acid, Body Arsenal, Breath of the Dragon, Song in
the Dark.

Four cards. One is rebounding damage, so can be played in addition to
a strike. One modifies strength AND does agg. One is useable at
close or long, but does damage at close (of course, the same set gave
Tzim the ability to prevent damage, so that's not too much of a
penaltY).

When the cards saw print, Tzimice were close-range fighters with a
smatting of long range (most environmental). The Assamites were
long-range fighters who could occasionally hit their mark hard. So,
when it came time to price the weapons, the Tzimice got the cheaper
cost because they don't benefit from the weapon nearly as much as the
Assamites do.

Even now, the Assamites didn't get any aggravated close range strikes,
where the Tzimice got Marauder. So the need for the Femur has reduced
even more.

The cards are balanced by the cards available, or absence thereof,
that grant similar effects to those clans.

Fanboy

> the Assamites have all of one source of close range aggravated damage,
> and it can't be played on the first round.
>
> Tzimice: Blood of Acid, Body Arsenal, Breath of the Dragon, Song in
> the Dark.

A reasonable comparison, but still the Assamites had access to Sengir
Dagger as a source of close range aggrivated damage. Fang did 2 aggro
damage (+ melee weapon bonues) where Sengir did 1 aggro (+ melee
weapon bonuses). Sengir cost 2 pool. Fang cost 3, but is clan
specific, which should have given a discount. At the time, 1 aggro
could burn someone, so it presumably wasn't getting the cost increase
that Flame Thrower was charged (i.e. the "I can burn you" premium).

In the end, I still blame the crack smoking--the AH designers figured
3 pool was ok for the Fang, and then the Sabbat designers figured that
2 pool was ok for the Tzimiscee. Fang should probably cost 2 pool too,
but no one, I figure, thought it was worth fixing.

-Peter
